title: Peer review is overwhelmed—can it survive in the AI era?
excerpt: As research and AI-assisted papers surge, volunteer reviewers struggle to keep up.
content_html:
peer pressure

As research and AI-assisted papers surge, volunteer reviewers struggle to keep up.

Credit: Aurich Lawson | Getty Images

Credit: Aurich Lawson | Getty Images

Jason Semprini was excited about his research on policies mandating that elementary school students receive the human papillomavirus vaccine. HPV causes most cases of cervical cancer, but counterintuitively, Semprini found that mandates don’t do that much to reduce the overall rate of cervical cancer in a population. That’s odd, but it’s also not completely surprising—we know that mandating a vaccine can motivate some people to find ways to avoid it.

Semprini wrote up the study and submitted the manuscript to a journal, where it was sent out for peer review, a long-standing process through which other researchers in the field assess the validity of research and make a recommendation on whether or not it should be published. This is usually done anonymously and on a volunteer basis.

In this case, the reviewer did not share Semprini’s excitement. That may have stemmed from a misunderstanding of the study’s central message: The reviewer mistakenly thought Semprini was questioning whether the HPV vaccine itself prevents cervical cancer rather than studying the effectiveness of a policy meant to increase vaccination rates. “There’s a very big difference there,” said Semprini, who is a health economist at Des Moines University.

Often, papers are reviewed by two or three experts, so if one misunderstands, the others can add clarity. But in this case, there was only one reviewer, so the paper was rejected.

It’s frustrating for Semprini to see his work held up because a reviewer didn’t read it carefully, and it’s an experience some researchers say is becoming increasingly common. Across disciplines, the number of publications is marching steadily upward. Reviewers are struggling to keep up, and the system appears to be faltering.

The number of papers indexed in the databases Scopus and Web of Science, for example, has recently been increasing exponentially, at a rate of 5.6 percent per year. By one estimate, researchers around the globe are devoting a collective 15,000 years of work to peer review every year—work that, if paid, would cost $1.5 billion for the share done in the US alone. Increasingly, researchers are finding it hard to donate that kind of time.

“I struggle like anything to get peer reviewers,” said Haseeb Irfanullah, who is on the editorial board of Wiley’s Learned Publishing but whose comments represent his own views as an independent consultant. Steven Mack, an editor for Human Immunology, has recently had to email around thirty researchers to find just one who would review a paper. Five years ago, he estimates it would have taken only five to 10 emails to find three willing reviewers. In this landscape, it’s not surprising that editors are assigning reviews to people who aren’t qualified or don’t have the time to concentrate on them.

In most fields, researchers need peer-reviewed publications to secure jobs and grants, so they continue to slog through the system even though it’s becoming “extremely protracted and painful,” in the words of microbiologist Sebastian Lourido from the Whitehead Institute.

Increasingly, many are advocating for change. Meanwhile, a few bold researchers have decided that the traditional publishing system just isn’t worth it anymore—AI research in particular has seen a shift toward communicating impactful findings through very informal means, like blogs.

Peer review is “the bedrock of science,” Semprini said. But at this moment, “it’s not standing strong.”

Newer than you think

Despite its central position in today’s research culture, peer review has been a universal feature of academic publishing for only about 50 years. Scientific societies had mechanisms for reviewing submissions and assessing their suitability for publication as long ago as the early 1800s, but their inner workings were variable, and the entire ethos of research was completely different at the time, says historian of science Aileen Fyfe from the University of St Andrews.

“Imagine all the people who are interested in astronomy in your country—and it’s not a very large number of people—but they all get together once a week on Thursday evenings to chat about astronomy, and they publish a journal together,” Fyfe told me, illustrating what science was like in the early days of reviewing.

Researchers were independent gentlemen rather than university professors, so publishing wasn’t tied to career progression. Moreover, working for a journal was a fun thing to do with friends, so they were usually happy to donate their time as reviewers.

Peer review became universal almost accidentally, as a way to solve a branding problem. In the 1970s, the US economy was tanking. Inflation was up, employment was down, there was a gas crisis, and the National Science Foundation found itself under public pressure to justify its spending.

The pressure followed a period of post-World War II enthusiasm for science during which federal funding increased 25-fold. The National Science Foundation had used external reviewers to assess grant applications since the 1950s—which was unusual at the time—and that turned out to be its saving grace. Because panels of independent reviewers decided how to allocate funding, their decisions had an air of legitimacy. Ultimately, that legitimacy was what kept lawmakers from putting the foundation’s funding decisions under their direct political control.

“It was really, in a lot of ways, a sales pitch from scientists to other stakeholders that made peer review into this cornerstone of science,” said Melinda Baldwin, a historian of science from the University of Maryland.

The United Kingdom went through a similar moment in the late 1980s and early 1990s when a number of controversial scientific issues—from HIV to the cause of autism to cold fusion—garnered a great deal of press attention. Suddenly, the public had an interest in distinguishing legitimate science from quackery, and a number of scientific organizations responded by saying, “We can tell what proper science looks like because proper science is peer reviewed,” Fyfe said.

Today, peer review is standard. Journal editors ask university professors to write reviews alongside a multitude of other professional responsibilities, and those requests often come at a quick clip. Lourido estimates he gets about 10 requests to review manuscripts each month, when realistically, he has time for only one or two. Mack receives a review request every day or two as part of his role as an immunogeneticist at the University of California, San Francisco (which he holds in addition to being a journal editor).

That cadence comes in part because more people are submitting studies to journals than ever before. But journals also proliferated between 1960 and 2020, and some regularly run “special issues,” for which researchers generate custom content. Many journals are also publishing more manuscripts because they’re now online-only, which frees editors from having to fit an issue onto a limited amount of paper.

Research is also increasingly interdisciplinary, meaning many studies require more knowledge and time to review. And AI contributes to the overload by making it easier for researchers to write up their work and easier for people from around the globe to submit to English-language journals. Then there are paper mills, or services that charge desperate researchers a fee to put their names on fabricated (but often legitimate-looking) publications.

All of this has made it difficult not only to maintain the quality of peer review but to ensure it happens at all. “Sometimes I think we need to start talking about the de-growth of publishing,” Irfanullah said. “It has grown like anything. It’s extremely unhealthy!”

Blogs are in

AI researchers are feeling the content explosion acutely. Computer scientists typically publish in conference proceedings, and the number of papers submitted to top AI conferences has increased between two- and 10-fold since 2019. As a result, it’s common to receive reviews from people who “just don’t understand the field enough to evaluate, or give good feedback,” says Haewon Jeong, a computer scientist from the University of California, Santa Barbara.

AI researchers are well-positioned to experiment with something different. Their field is new, it’s moving lightning-fast, and much of the work is taking place outside academia, so many researchers don’t need formal publications for their career progression. Against this backdrop, blogs have taken off. These days, “maintaining a good blog is almost like having a good podcast channel,” Jeong said. “Your voice gets really amplified, and you get known.”

Many blogs are written by industry leaders, but some academics are also jumping on the bandwagon. Helen Qu, an AI researcher from the Flatiron Institute, came to hate the unrewarding grind of conference submissions so much that she has decided to publish her research only on her new blog (she’s currently working on using game theory to prevent AI from acting subversively).

One long-running blog, called the AI Alignment Forum, is written by a wide community of researchers, including many academics, who are concerned with how to make AI safe and beneficial to humanity. Instead of peer review, the AI Alignment Forum uses a mechanism that allows members to upvote or downvote content and post comments to explain their views.

Of course, there’s no guarantee that readers have put much, if any, thought into an up- or downvote. “That’s one of the big weaknesses of it,” acknowledged Oliver Habryka, the CEO of Lightcone Infrastructure, which runs the AI Alignment Forum.

On the other hand, posts tend to get many more reactions than the handful of peer reviews they would receive at a journal. And readers can alter their votes after reacting to comments. Another way the AI Alignment Forum tries to highlight quality work is by revisiting the year’s top content and asking members to write commentaries on how it’s aged and whether the claims have held up.

The system offers several advantages over traditional publishing. First, it’s much, much faster, which is especially important in a quickly moving field. Often, if a researcher submits to a traditional journal, “by the time your thing passes peer review, there’s a very substantial chance it’s already out of date,” Habryka said.

But perhaps an even stronger advantage of the AI Alignment Forum, in Habryka’s view, is that the voting system draws readers’ attention to both good research and to the counter-arguments against it. Without such a mechanism, many researchers would rely on social media to highlight what’s up-and-coming. But that puts a field’s focus at the whim of companies that use proprietary, potentially biased, and often opaque mechanisms to decide which content to feature prominently. “I really don’t want the attention of my field to be downstream of the Twitter algorithm,” Habryka said.

The colloquial writing style used on many blogs can also draw attention, which comes with pros and cons. For Qu, it means she doesn’t have to worry as much about someone else getting credit for her ideas when she publishes on her blog because nobody will put quite the same personal slant on the work that she will. And Jeong thinks the accessible style can make complex concepts easier to understand. “There’s value in that,” she said.

But philosopher David Thorstad from Vanderbilt University cautions that accessibility could come at the expense of rigor and that colloquial writing could let charismatic voices rise to the top regardless of the quality of their work.

Moving away from peer review can also isolate your work, Thorstad said. He studies longtermerism: how to best protect the people of the future. Lately, many longtermists have been concerned about how to prevent AI from bringing about the downfall of humanity, and many have published their work on the AI Alignment Forum.

That poses a problem for Thorstad, who is a strong believer in peer review and publishes only in venues that use it. Citing work that wasn’t peer-reviewed is sure to raise red flags, given that his own work has to go through the review process in those venues. That means he can’t cite a large segment of the work in his field. “It’s incredibly limiting,” he said.

Five years ago, this was a bigger problem than it is today, Habryka said. Now, reviewers in most disciplines accept that there are various ways to publish legitimate work. “I think less than 50 percent of things you really want to cite in [a machine learning] paper end up actually being properly peer reviewed,” he said.

Changing tactics

With peer review still taking up a lot of time, plenty of researchers are looking for shortcuts to speed up the process. A survey conducted by staff at the Frontiers journals found that over half of peer reviewers already incorporate AI into the process in some way, probably at least partly for this reason.

One day, AI-produced reviews may be seen as routine and beneficial. But at the moment, AI is often used in ways researchers find annoying and unethical. Linguist Marijn van Putten from Leiden University, for instance, was initially excited to receive a review suggesting he cite a particular medieval Arabic manual in his publication about which ancient religious leader put forward a particular interpretation of the Qur’an. “I was like, ‘That’s great, I’m going to look it up!’” he said.

But he couldn’t track down the reference anywhere. Finally, after two days of searching, van Putten started to consider another possibility: that AI had hallucinated the reference. He went back to the review and noticed that, indeed, it contained hallmarks of AI-generated text, such as the gratuitous use of em dashes. He ran the text through an AI detection tool, which told him it was almost certainly generated by AI. “It was very frustrating and a colossal waste of my time,” he said.

In addition to the risk of hallucinations, uploading an unpublished manuscript to a chatbot that may retain the data could constitute a breach of confidentiality, says Chris ChoGlueck, a philosopher at New Mexico Tech. Locally run large language models or services that agree not to retain the data could provide solutions, but they require that someone who is demonstrating a willingness to take shortcuts also exercise a degree of care.

This year, the AI conference NeurIPS will run a trial to see if a custom AI tool can help reviewers without replacing their judgment entirely. For example, the tool could help researchers understand the submission and do the background research necessary to write the review, but it would not write the review itself, conference organizers wrote on the NeurIPS website.

Meanwhile, many fields are experimenting with other ways of reforming peer review. One long-standing tactic to address the slow review process involves preprints—formally written publications that researchers post on a site such as arxiv.org so that their research is visible while they navigate the usual publishing process. Preprints are now seen as a legitimate basis for grant and job applications in some fields because it’s widely understood that people shouldn’t have to hit pause on their careers while they wait for formal publication.

Other ideas focus on the review process itself. One obvious step is to redistribute the review workload to reflect the source of submissions. Editors tend to disproportionately assign reviews to male researchers from the United States and a handful of other countries rather than distributing the workload equitably.

Some researchers also advocate for paying peer reviewers, though others worry that the practice would increase the burdensome publication fees researchers already face. There is evidence that compensation in the $100–$300 range per review speeds up the process without compromising quality. That could be because adding money to the equation makes it feel like “there’s actually a hard deadline,” said ChoGlueck.

Without that motivation, some reviewers might view deadlines as “magical,” he suggested, “because you can just change them.”

Others are pushing for more structural change. One option, which is already in use on a limited basis, is to divorce the peer-review process from journal submission. Rather, a community of researchers reviews papers before they’re formally submitted, and researchers can then choose to submit their papers to a number of journals that have committed to publishing studies reviewed this way. If the first journal decides not to publish an article, the authors can approach a second journal without having to undergo a new round of peer review.

Meanwhile, scholarly communication advocate Cameron Neylon has long been on the record as questioning whether all journal articles really need peer review, given how few papers end up having an impact on the world. Maybe, he suggests, studies should have to meet a threshold of interest before they’re sent out for peer review.

With all these pressures and propositions, is peer review nearing a breaking point, and will it ultimately fail?

It’s hard to envision a wholesale shift away from peer review because the system is so firmly entrenched in most fields, both as part of career progression and as a way of garnering public trust. At the same time, if academic publishing keeps growing at the rate it has been, the system simply won’t be able to keep up. “So something’s going to break there at some point,” Neylon said. It’s just as hard to envision researchers voluntarily publishing less, given current incentives. But maybe both will happen to some degree. With the pool of reviewers being tapped out, journals will have to curb their proliferation, which could temper the rise in publications. There’s already evidence of these last two things happening. Peer review is resilient, if not unflappable. The practice will probably stick around in one form or another, but it might not be the same peer review we’re used to.

blocks.html_en: Jason Semprini was excited about his research on policies mandating that elementary school students receive the human papillomavirus vaccine. HPV causes most cases of cervical cancer, but counterintuitively, Semprini found that mandates don’t do that much to reduce the overall rate of cervical cancer in a population. That’s odd, but it’s also not completely surprising—we know that mandating a vaccine can motivate some people to find ways to avoid it.

sentences.en: Jason Semprini was excited about his research on policies mandating that elementary school students receive the human papillomavirus vaccine.
sentences.zh: Jason Semprini 对他关于强制小学生接种人乳头瘤病毒疫苗的政策研究感到兴奋。

sentences.en: HPV causes most cases of cervical cancer, but counterintuitively, Semprini found that mandates don’t do that much to reduce the overall rate of cervical cancer in a population.
sentences.zh: HPV 会导致大多数宫颈癌病例，但与直觉相反的是，Semprini 发现强制措施对于降低人群中宫颈癌的总体发病率并没有多大作用。

sentences.en: That’s odd, but it’s also not completely surprising—we know that mandating a vaccine can motivate some people to find ways to avoid it.
sentences.zh: 这很奇怪，但也并不完全令人惊讶——我们知道强制接种疫苗可以激励一些人找到避免疫苗的方法。

blocks.html_en: Semprini wrote up the study and submitted the manuscript to a journal, where it was sent out for peer review, a long-standing process through which other researchers in the field assess the validity of research and make a recommendation on whether or not it should be published. This is usually done anonymously and on a volunteer basis.

sentences.en: Semprini wrote up the study and submitted the manuscript to a journal, where it was sent out for peer review, a long-standing process through which other researchers in the field assess the validity of research and make a recommendation on whether or not it should be published.
sentences.zh: 森普里尼撰写了这项研究，并将手稿提交给一家期刊，然后将其发送给同行评审，这是一个长期的过程，该领域的其他研究人员通过该过程评估研究的有效性，并就是否应该发表该研究提出建议。

sentences.en: This is usually done anonymously and on a volunteer basis.
sentences.zh: 这通常是匿名且在志愿者的基础上完成的。

blocks.html_en: In this case, the reviewer did not share Semprini’s excitement. That may have stemmed from a misunderstanding of the study’s central message: The reviewer mistakenly thought Semprini was questioning whether the HPV vaccine itself prevents cervical cancer rather than studying the effectiveness of a policy meant to increase vaccination rates. “There’s a very big difference there,” said Semprini, who is a health economist at Des Moines University.

sentences.en: In this case, the reviewer did not share Semprini’s excitement.
sentences.zh: 在这种情况下，审稿人并不像森普里尼那样兴奋。

sentences.en: That may have stemmed from a misunderstanding of the study’s central message: The reviewer mistakenly thought Semprini was questioning whether the HPV vaccine itself prevents cervical cancer rather than studying the effectiveness of a policy meant to increase vaccination rates.
sentences.zh: 这可能源于对该研究中心信息的误解：审稿人错误地认为 Semprini 是在质疑 HPV 疫苗本身是否可以预防宫颈癌，而不是在研究旨在提高疫苗接种率的政策的有效性。

sentences.en: “There’s a very big difference there,” said Semprini, who is a health economist at Des Moines University.
sentences.zh: 得梅因大学健康经济学家森普里尼说：“两者之间存在很大差异。”

blocks.html_en: Often, papers are reviewed by two or three experts, so if one misunderstands, the others can add clarity. But in this case, there was only one reviewer, so the paper was rejected.

sentences.en: Often, papers are reviewed by two or three experts, so if one misunderstands, the others can add clarity.
sentences.zh: 通常，论文由两到三名专家审阅，因此如果其中一位专家产生误解，其他人可以澄清。

sentences.en: But in this case, there was only one reviewer, so the paper was rejected.
sentences.zh: 但在这种情况下，只有一名审稿人，所以论文被拒绝了。

blocks.html_en: It’s frustrating for Semprini to see his work held up because a reviewer didn’t read it carefully, and it’s an experience some researchers say is becoming increasingly common. Across disciplines, the number of publications is marching steadily upward. Reviewers are struggling to keep up, and the system appears to be faltering.

sentences.en: It’s frustrating for Semprini to see his work held up because a reviewer didn’t read it carefully, and it’s an experience some researchers say is becoming increasingly common.
sentences.zh: 塞姆普里尼看到自己的作品因为审稿人没有仔细阅读而被搁置，这让他感到沮丧，一些研究人员表示，这种经历正变得越来越普遍。

sentences.en: Across disciplines, the number of publications is marching steadily upward.
sentences.zh: 在各个学科中，出版物的数量正在稳步上升。

sentences.en: Reviewers are struggling to keep up, and the system appears to be faltering.
sentences.zh: 审稿人正在努力跟上，系统似乎摇摇欲坠。

blocks.html_en: The number of papers indexed in the databases Scopus and Web of Science, for example, has recently been increasing exponentially, at a rate of 5.6 percent per year. By one estimate, researchers around the globe are devoting a collective 15,000 years of work to peer review every year—work that, if paid, would cost $1.5 billion for the share done in the US alone. Increasingly, researchers are finding it hard to donate that kind of time.

sentences.en: The number of papers indexed in the databases Scopus and Web of Science, for example, has recently been increasing exponentially, at a rate of 5.6 percent per year.
sentences.zh: 例如，Scopus 和 Web of Science 数据库中索引的论文数量最近呈指数增长，每年增长 5.6%。

sentences.en: By one estimate, researchers around the globe are devoting a collective 15,000 years of work to peer review every year—work that, if paid, would cost $1.5 billion for the share done in the US alone.
sentences.zh: 据估计，全球研究人员每年都会在同行评审上投入总计 15,000 年的工作——如果支付费用，仅在美国完成的工作就需要花费 15 亿美元。

sentences.en: Increasingly, researchers are finding it hard to donate that kind of time.
sentences.zh: 研究人员越来越发现很难贡献出这样的时间。

blocks.html_en: “I struggle like anything to get peer reviewers,” said Haseeb Irfanullah, who is on the editorial board of Wiley’s Learned Publishing but whose comments represent his own views as an independent consultant. Steven Mack, an editor for Human Immunology, has recently had to email around thirty researchers to find just one who would review a paper. Five years ago, he estimates it would have taken only five to 10 emails to find three willing reviewers. In this landscape, it’s not surprising that editors are assigning reviews to people who aren’t qualified or don’t have the time to concentrate on them.

sentences.en: “I struggle like anything to get peer reviewers,” said Haseeb Irfanullah, who is on the editorial board of Wiley’s Learned Publishing but whose comments represent his own views as an independent consultant.
sentences.zh: “我竭力争取同行评审，”哈西布·伊法努拉 (Haseeb Irfanullah) 说道，他是 Wiley’s Learned Publishing 的编辑委员会成员，但他的评论代表了他作为独立顾问的个人观点。

sentences.en: Steven Mack, an editor for Human Immunology, has recently had to email around thirty researchers to find just one who would review a paper.
sentences.zh: 《人类免疫学》的编辑史蒂文·麦克 (Steven Mack) 最近不得不向大约 30 位研究人员发送电子邮件，以找到一位愿意审阅论文的人。

sentences.en: Five years ago, he estimates it would have taken only five to 10 emails to find three willing reviewers.
sentences.zh: 五年前，他估计只需要 5 到 10 封电子邮件就能找到三位愿意的审稿人。

sentences.en: In this landscape, it’s not surprising that editors are assigning reviews to people who aren’t qualified or don’t have the time to concentrate on them.
sentences.zh: 在这种情况下，编辑将审稿分配给不合格或没有时间专注于他们的人也就不足为奇了。

blocks.html_en: In most fields, researchers need peer-reviewed publications to secure jobs and grants, so they continue to slog through the system even though it’s becoming “extremely protracted and painful,” in the words of microbiologist Sebastian Lourido from the Whitehead Institute.

sentences.en: In most fields, researchers need peer-reviewed publications to secure jobs and grants, so they continue to slog through the system even though it’s becoming “extremely protracted and painful,” in the words of microbiologist Sebastian Lourido from the Whitehead Institute.
sentences.zh: 在大多数领域，研究人员需要经过同行评审的出版物来获得工作和资助，因此他们继续在这个系统中艰难前行，尽管用怀特海研究所的微生物学家塞巴斯蒂安·卢里多的话说，这个过程变得“极其漫长和痛苦”。

blocks.html_en: Increasingly, many are advocating for change. Meanwhile, a few bold researchers have decided that the traditional publishing system just isn’t worth it anymore—AI research in particular has seen a shift toward communicating impactful findings through very informal means, like blogs.

sentences.en: Increasingly, many are advocating for change.
sentences.zh: 越来越多的人提倡变革。

sentences.en: Meanwhile, a few bold researchers have decided that the traditional publishing system just isn’t worth it anymore—AI research in particular has seen a shift toward communicating impactful findings through very informal means, like blogs.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，一些大胆的研究人员认为传统的出版系统已经不再值得了——尤其是人工智能研究已经转向通过博客等非常非正式的方式交流有影响力的发现。

blocks.html_en: Peer review is “the bedrock of science,” Semprini said. But at this moment, “it’s not standing strong.”

sentences.en: Peer review is “the bedrock of science,” Semprini said.
sentences.zh: 森普里尼说，同行评审是“科学的基石”。

sentences.en: But at this moment, “it’s not standing strong.”
sentences.zh: 但此时此刻，“它还没有站稳脚跟”。

blocks.html_en: Newer than you think

sentences.en: Newer than you think
sentences.zh: 比你想象的更新

blocks.html_en: Despite its central position in today’s research culture, peer review has been a universal feature of academic publishing for only about 50 years. Scientific societies had mechanisms for reviewing submissions and assessing their suitability for publication as long ago as the early 1800s, but their inner workings were variable, and the entire ethos of research was completely different at the time, says historian of science Aileen Fyfe from the University of St Andrews.

sentences.en: Despite its central position in today’s research culture, peer review has been a universal feature of academic publishing for only about 50 years.
sentences.zh: 尽管同行评审在当今的研究文化中占据着核心地位，但它成为学术出版的普遍特征仅约 50 年。

sentences.en: Scientific societies had mechanisms for reviewing submissions and assessing their suitability for publication as long ago as the early 1800s, but their inner workings were variable, and the entire ethos of research was completely different at the time, says historian of science Aileen Fyfe from the University of St Andrews.
sentences.zh: 圣安德鲁斯大学的科学史学家艾琳·法伊夫 (Aileen Fyfe) 表示，早在 1800 年代初，科学协会就有了审查提交内容并评估其是否适合发表的机制，但其内部运作方式各不相同，而且当时的整个研究精神也完全不同。

blocks.html_en: “Imagine all the people who are interested in astronomy in your country—and it’s not a very large number of people—but they all get together once a week on Thursday evenings to chat about astronomy, and they publish a journal together,” Fyfe told me, illustrating what science was like in the early days of reviewing.

sentences.en: “Imagine all the people who are interested in astronomy in your country—and it’s not a very large number of people—but they all get together once a week on Thursday evenings to chat about astronomy, and they publish a journal together,” Fyfe told me, illustrating what science was like in the early days of reviewing.
sentences.zh: “想象一下你们国家所有对天文学感兴趣的人——人数不是很多——但他们每周四晚上都会聚在一起讨论天文学，并一起出版一本期刊，”费夫告诉我，这说明了科学在早期的审稿中是什么样子。

blocks.html_en: Researchers were independent gentlemen rather than university professors, so publishing wasn’t tied to career progression. Moreover, working for a journal was a fun thing to do with friends, so they were usually happy to donate their time as reviewers.

sentences.en: Researchers were independent gentlemen rather than university professors, so publishing wasn’t tied to career progression.
sentences.zh: 研究人员是独立的绅士而不是大学教授，因此出版与职业发展无关。

sentences.en: Moreover, working for a journal was a fun thing to do with friends, so they were usually happy to donate their time as reviewers.
sentences.zh: 此外，与朋友一起为期刊工作是一件有趣的事情，因此他们通常很乐意贡献自己的时间作为审稿人。

blocks.html_en: Peer review became universal almost accidentally, as a way to solve a branding problem. In the 1970s, the US economy was tanking. Inflation was up, employment was down, there was a gas crisis, and the National Science Foundation found itself under public pressure to justify its spending.

sentences.en: Peer review became universal almost accidentally, as a way to solve a branding problem.
sentences.zh: 作为解决品牌问题的一种方式，同行评审几乎是意外地变得普遍。

sentences.en: In the 1970s, the US economy was tanking.
sentences.zh: 20世纪70年代，美国经济陷入低迷。

sentences.en: Inflation was up, employment was down, there was a gas crisis, and the National Science Foundation found itself under public pressure to justify its spending.
sentences.zh: 通货膨胀上升，就业下降，出现天然气危机，国家科学基金会发现自己面临公众压力，要求其支出合理。

blocks.html_en: The pressure followed a period of post-World War II enthusiasm for science during which federal funding increased 25-fold. The National Science Foundation had used external reviewers to assess grant applications since the 1950s—which was unusual at the time—and that turned out to be its saving grace. Because panels of independent reviewers decided how to allocate funding, their decisions had an air of legitimacy. Ultimately, that legitimacy was what kept lawmakers from putting the foundation’s funding decisions under their direct political control.

sentences.en: The pressure followed a period of post-World War II enthusiasm for science during which federal funding increased 25-fold.
sentences.zh: 这种压力源于二战后一段时期的科学热情，在此期间联邦资助增加了 25 倍。

sentences.en: The National Science Foundation had used external reviewers to assess grant applications since the 1950s—which was unusual at the time—and that turned out to be its saving grace.
sentences.zh: 自 20 世纪 50 年代以来，美国国家科学基金会一直聘请外部评审员来评估资助申请（这在当时是不寻常的），但事实证明，这成为了它的可取之处。

sentences.en: Because panels of independent reviewers decided how to allocate funding, their decisions had an air of legitimacy.
sentences.zh: 由于独立审查小组决定如何分配资金，他们的决定具有合法性。

sentences.en: Ultimately, that legitimacy was what kept lawmakers from putting the foundation’s funding decisions under their direct political control.
sentences.zh: 最终，这种合法性阻止了立法者将基金会的资助决策置于直接政治控制之下。

blocks.html_en: “It was really, in a lot of ways, a sales pitch from scientists to other stakeholders that made peer review into this cornerstone of science,” said Melinda Baldwin, a historian of science from the University of Maryland.

sentences.en: “It was really, in a lot of ways, a sales pitch from scientists to other stakeholders that made peer review into this cornerstone of science,” said Melinda Baldwin, a historian of science from the University of Maryland.
sentences.zh: 马里兰大学科学史学家梅琳达·鲍德温 (Melinda Baldwin) 表示：“在很多方面，这实际上是科学家向其他利益相关者进行的推销，将同行评审纳入了科学的基石。”

blocks.html_en: The United Kingdom went through a similar moment in the late 1980s and early 1990s when a number of controversial scientific issues—from HIV to the cause of autism to cold fusion—garnered a great deal of press attention. Suddenly, the public had an interest in distinguishing legitimate science from quackery, and a number of scientific organizations responded by saying, “We can tell what proper science looks like because proper science is peer reviewed,” Fyfe said.

sentences.en: The United Kingdom went through a similar moment in the late 1980s and early 1990s when a number of controversial scientific issues—from HIV to the cause of autism to cold fusion—garnered a great deal of press attention.
sentences.zh: 英国在 20 世纪 80 年代末和 90 年代初也经历过类似的时刻，当时许多有争议的科学问题——从艾滋病毒到自闭症的病因，再到冷聚变——引起了媒体的广泛关注。

sentences.en: Suddenly, the public had an interest in distinguishing legitimate science from quackery, and a number of scientific organizations responded by saying, “We can tell what proper science looks like because proper science is peer reviewed,” Fyfe said.
sentences.zh: 突然间，公众对区分合法科学和庸医产生了兴趣，许多科学组织回应说，“我们可以分辨什么是正确的科学，因为正确的科学是经过同行评审的，”费夫说。

blocks.html_en: Today, peer review is standard. Journal editors ask university professors to write reviews alongside a multitude of other professional responsibilities, and those requests often come at a quick clip. Lourido estimates he gets about 10 requests to review manuscripts each month, when realistically, he has time for only one or two. Mack receives a review request every day or two as part of his role as an immunogeneticist at the University of California, San Francisco (which he holds in addition to being a journal editor).

sentences.en: Today, peer review is standard.
sentences.zh: 如今，同行评审已成为标准。

sentences.en: Journal editors ask university professors to write reviews alongside a multitude of other professional responsibilities, and those requests often come at a quick clip.
sentences.zh: 期刊编辑要求大学教授在承担众多其他专业职责的同时撰写评论，而这些要求通常很快就会到来。

sentences.en: Lourido estimates he gets about 10 requests to review manuscripts each month, when realistically, he has time for only one or two.
sentences.zh: Lourido 估计他每个月会收到大约 10 个审稿请求，而实际上，他只有一两个时间。

sentences.en: Mack receives a review request every day or two as part of his role as an immunogeneticist at the University of California, San Francisco (which he holds in addition to being a journal editor).
sentences.zh: 作为加州大学旧金山分校免疫遗传学家（他除了担任期刊编辑之外）的一部分，麦克每一两天都会收到审稿请求。

blocks.html_en: That cadence comes in part because more people are submitting studies to journals than ever before. But journals also proliferated between 1960 and 2020, and some regularly run “special issues,” for which researchers generate custom content. Many journals are also publishing more manuscripts because they’re now online-only, which frees editors from having to fit an issue onto a limited amount of paper.

sentences.en: That cadence comes in part because more people are submitting studies to journals than ever before.
sentences.zh: 这种节奏的部分原因是越来越多的人向期刊提交研究成果。

sentences.en: But journals also proliferated between 1960 and 2020, and some regularly run “special issues,” for which researchers generate custom content.
sentences.zh: 但 1960 年至 2020 年间，期刊数量也激增，其中一些定期出版“特刊”，研究人员为其生成定制内容。

sentences.en: Many journals are also publishing more manuscripts because they’re now online-only, which frees editors from having to fit an issue onto a limited amount of paper.
sentences.zh: 许多期刊还发表了更多的手稿，因为它们现在只在网上发布，这使得编辑不必将一期文章放在有限的纸张上。

blocks.html_en: Research is also increasingly interdisciplinary, meaning many studies require more knowledge and time to review. And AI contributes to the overload by making it easier for researchers to write up their work and easier for people from around the globe to submit to English-language journals. Then there are paper mills, or services that charge desperate researchers a fee to put their names on fabricated (but often legitimate-looking) publications.

sentences.en: Research is also increasingly interdisciplinary, meaning many studies require more knowledge and time to review.
sentences.zh: 研究也越来越跨学科，这意味着许多研究需要更多的知识和时间来审查。

sentences.en: And AI contributes to the overload by making it easier for researchers to write up their work and easier for people from around the globe to submit to English-language journals.
sentences.zh: 人工智能让研究人员更容易撰写他们的研究成果，也让世界各地的人们更容易向英文期刊提交论文，从而加剧了超载。

sentences.en: Then there are paper mills, or services that charge desperate researchers a fee to put their names on fabricated (but often legitimate-looking) publications.
sentences.zh: 还有一些造纸厂或服务机构向绝望的研究人员收取费用，让他们将自己的名字印在伪造的（但通常看起来合法的）出版物上。

blocks.html_en: All of this has made it difficult not only to maintain the quality of peer review but to ensure it happens at all. “Sometimes I think we need to start talking about the de-growth of publishing,” Irfanullah said. “It has grown like anything. It’s extremely unhealthy!”

sentences.en: All of this has made it difficult not only to maintain the quality of peer review but to ensure it happens at all.
sentences.zh: 所有这些使得不仅难以维持同行评审的质量，而且难以确保同行评审的发生。

sentences.en: “Sometimes I think we need to start talking about the de-growth of publishing,” Irfanullah said.
sentences.zh: “有时我认为我们需要开始讨论出版业的低增长问题，”伊尔法努拉说。

sentences.en: “It has grown like anything.
sentences.zh: “它已经像任何东西一样成长了。

sentences.en: It’s extremely unhealthy!”
sentences.zh: 这是极其不健康的！”

sentences.en: Blogs are in
sentences.zh: 博客位于

blocks.html_en: AI researchers are feeling the content explosion acutely. Computer scientists typically publish in conference proceedings, and the number of papers submitted to top AI conferences has increased between two- and 10-fold since 2019. As a result, it’s common to receive reviews from people who “just don’t understand the field enough to evaluate, or give good feedback,” says Haewon Jeong, a computer scientist from the University of California, Santa Barbara.

sentences.en: AI researchers are feeling the content explosion acutely.
sentences.zh: 人工智能研究人员敏锐地感受到内容爆炸式增长。

sentences.en: Computer scientists typically publish in conference proceedings, and the number of papers submitted to top AI conferences has increased between two- and 10-fold since 2019.
sentences.zh: 计算机科学家通常在会议论文集上发表论文，自 2019 年以来，提交给顶级人工智能会议的论文数量增加了 2 至 10 倍。

sentences.en: As a result, it’s common to receive reviews from people who “just don’t understand the field enough to evaluate, or give good feedback,” says Haewon Jeong, a computer scientist from the University of California, Santa Barbara.
sentences.zh: 因此，经常会收到来自“对这个领域不够了解，无法进行评估或提供良好反馈”的人的评论，加州大学圣塔芭芭拉分校的计算机科学家 Haewon Jeong 表示。

blocks.html_en: AI researchers are well-positioned to experiment with something different. Their field is new, it’s moving lightning-fast, and much of the work is taking place outside academia, so many researchers don’t need formal publications for their career progression. Against this backdrop, blogs have taken off. These days, “maintaining a good blog is almost like having a good podcast channel,” Jeong said. “Your voice gets really amplified, and you get known.”

sentences.en: AI researchers are well-positioned to experiment with something different.
sentences.zh: 人工智能研究人员有能力尝试不同的东西。

sentences.en: Their field is new, it’s moving lightning-fast, and much of the work is taking place outside academia, so many researchers don’t need formal publications for their career progression.
sentences.zh: 他们的领域是新的，发展速度快如闪电，而且大部分工作都是在学术界之外进行的，因此许多研究人员不需要正式的出版物来促进他们的职业发展。

sentences.en: Against this backdrop, blogs have taken off.
sentences.zh: 在此背景下，博客蓬勃发展。

sentences.en: These days, “maintaining a good blog is almost like having a good podcast channel,” Jeong said.
sentences.zh: 如今，“维护一个好的博客几乎就像拥有一个好的播客频道一样，”郑说。

sentences.en: “Your voice gets really amplified, and you get known.”

blocks.html_en: It’s hard to envision a wholesale shift away from peer review because the system is so firmly entrenched in most fields, both as part of career progression and as a way of garnering public trust. At the same time, if academic publishing keeps growing at the rate it has been, the system simply won’t be able to keep up. “So something’s going to break there at some point,” Neylon said. Instead of dropping peer review, he suggests that maybe research fields should find ways to encourage quality publications over quantity.

sentences.en: It’s hard to envision a wholesale shift away from peer review because the system is so firmly entrenched in most fields, both as part of career progression and as a way of garnering public trust.
sentences.zh: 很难想象全面放弃同行评审，因为该系统在大多数领域都根深蒂固，既是职业发展的一部分，也是获得公众信任的一种方式。

sentences.en: At the same time, if academic publishing keeps growing at the rate it has been, the system simply won’t be able to keep up.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，如果学术出版继续以目前的速度增长，系统根本无法跟上。

sentences.en: “So something’s going to break there at some point,” Neylon said.
sentences.zh: “所以在某个时刻，有些东西会崩溃，”尼伦说。

sentences.en: Instead of dropping peer review, he suggests that maybe research fields should find ways to encourage quality publications over quantity.
sentences.zh: 他建议，也许研究领域应该找到方法来鼓励高质量的出版物而不是数量，而不是放弃同行评审。

blocks.html_en: It’s just as hard to envision researchers voluntarily publishing less, given current incentives. But maybe both will happen to some degree. With the pool of reviewers being tapped out, journals will have to curb their proliferation, which could temper the rise in publications. Meanwhile, peer review may become a less rigorous, more fragmented version of what it once was, with the practice taking on different meanings in different fields.

sentences.en: It’s just as hard to envision researchers voluntarily publishing less, given current incentives.
sentences.zh: 考虑到目前的激励措施，很难想象研究人员会自愿减少发表论文。

sentences.en: But maybe both will happen to some degree.
sentences.zh: 但也许两者都会在某种程度上发生。

sentences.en: With the pool of reviewers being tapped out, journals will have to curb their proliferation, which could temper the rise in publications.
sentences.zh: 随着审稿人数量的减少，期刊将不得不遏制审稿人的激增，这可能会抑制出版物数量的增长。

sentences.en: Meanwhile, peer review may become a less rigorous, more fragmented version of what it once was, with the practice taking on different meanings in different fields.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，同行评审可能会变得不那么严格、更加碎片化，这种做法在不同领域具有不同的含义。

blocks.html_en: There’s already evidence of these last two things happening. It used to be standard for three reviewers to review manuscripts, but Mack says he’s lately seen the average in immunology move closer to two. In economics, some prominent journals already pay peer reviewers. Meanwhile, researchers in many scientific fields routinely publish preprints.

sentences.en: There’s already evidence of these last two things happening.
sentences.zh: 已经有证据表明后两件事正在发生。

sentences.en: It used to be standard for three reviewers to review manuscripts, but Mack says he’s lately seen the average in immunology move closer to two.
sentences.zh: 过去，三名审稿人审稿是标准做法，但麦克说，他最近发现免疫学领域的平均审稿人数量接近两名。

sentences.en: In economics, some prominent journals already pay peer reviewers.
sentences.zh: 在经济学领域，一些著名期刊已经向同行评审员支付费用。

sentences.en: Meanwhile, researchers in many scientific fields routinely publish preprints.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，许多科学领域的研究人员经常发布预印本。

blocks.html_en: Peer review is resilient, if not unflappable. The practice will probably stick around in one form or another, but it might not be the same peer review we’re used to.

同侪压力

随着研究和人工智能辅助论文的激增，志愿审稿人很难跟上。

图片来源：Aurich Lawson |盖蒂图片社

图片来源：Aurich Lawson |盖蒂图片社

Jason Semprini 对他关于强制小学生接种人乳头瘤病毒疫苗的政策研究感到兴奋。 HPV 会导致大多数宫颈癌病例，但与直觉相反的是，Semprini 发现强制措施对于降低人群中宫颈癌的总体发病率并没有多大作用。 这很奇怪，但也并不完全令人惊讶——我们知道强制接种疫苗可以激励一些人找到避免疫苗的方法。

森普里尼撰写了这项研究，并将手稿提交给一家期刊，然后将其发送给同行评审，这是一个长期的过程，该领域的其他研究人员通过该过程评估研究的有效性，并就是否应该发表该研究提出建议。 这通常是匿名且在志愿者的基础上完成的。

在这种情况下，审稿人并不像森普里尼那样兴奋。 这可能源于对该研究中心信息的误解：审稿人错误地认为 Semprini 是在质疑 HPV 疫苗本身是否可以预防宫颈癌，而不是在研究旨在提高疫苗接种率的政策的有效性。 得梅因大学健康经济学家森普里尼说：“两者之间存在很大差异。”

通常，论文由两到三名专家审阅，因此如果其中一位专家产生误解，其他人可以澄清。 但在这种情况下，只有一名审稿人，所以论文被拒绝了。

塞姆普里尼看到自己的作品因为审稿人没有仔细阅读而被搁置，这让他感到沮丧，一些研究人员表示，这种经历正变得越来越普遍。 在各个学科中，出版物的数量正在稳步上升。 审稿人正在努力跟上，系统似乎摇摇欲坠。

例如，Scopus 和 Web of Science 数据库中索引的论文数量最近呈指数增长，每年增长 5.6%。 据估计，全球研究人员每年都会在同行评审上投入总计 15,000 年的工作——如果支付费用，仅在美国完成的工作就需要花费 15 亿美元。 研究人员越来越发现很难贡献出这样的时间。

“我竭力争取同行评审，”哈西布·伊法努拉 (Haseeb Irfanullah) 说道，他是 Wiley’s Learned Publishing 的编辑委员会成员，但他的评论代表了他作为独立顾问的个人观点。 《人类免疫学》的编辑史蒂文·麦克 (Steven Mack) 最近不得不向大约 30 位研究人员发送电子邮件，以找到一位愿意审阅论文的人。 五年前，他估计只需要 5 到 10 封电子邮件就能找到三位愿意的审稿人。 在这种情况下，编辑将审稿分配给不合格或没有时间专注于他们的人也就不足为奇了。

在大多数领域，研究人员需要经过同行评审的出版物来获得工作和资助，因此他们继续在这个系统中艰难前行，尽管用怀特海研究所的微生物学家塞巴斯蒂安·卢里多的话说，这个过程变得“极其漫长和痛苦”。

越来越多的人提倡变革。 与此同时，一些大胆的研究人员认为传统的出版系统已经不再值得了——尤其是人工智能研究已经转向通过博客等非常非正式的方式交流有影响力的发现。

森普里尼说，同行评审是“科学的基石”。 但此时此刻，“它还没有站稳脚跟”。

比你想象的更新

尽管同行评审在当今的研究文化中占据着核心地位，但它成为学术出版的普遍特征仅约 50 年。 圣安德鲁斯大学的科学史学家艾琳·法伊夫 (Aileen Fyfe) 表示，早在 1800 年代初，科学协会就有了审查提交内容并评估其是否适合发表的机制，但其内部运作方式各不相同，而且当时的整个研究精神也完全不同。

“想象一下你们国家所有对天文学感兴趣的人——人数不是很多——但他们每周四晚上都会聚在一起讨论天文学，并一起出版一本期刊，”费夫告诉我，这说明了科学在早期的审稿中是什么样子。

研究人员是独立的绅士而不是大学教授，因此出版与职业发展无关。 此外，与朋友一起为期刊工作是一件有趣的事情，因此他们通常很乐意贡献自己的时间作为审稿人。

作为解决品牌问题的一种方式，同行评审几乎是意外地变得普遍。 20世纪70年代，美国经济陷入低迷。 通货膨胀上升，就业下降，出现天然气危机，国家科学基金会发现自己面临公众压力，要求其支出合理。

这种压力源于二战后一段时期的科学热情，在此期间联邦资助增加了 25 倍。 自 20 世纪 50 年代以来，美国国家科学基金会一直聘请外部评审员来评估资助申请（这在当时是不寻常的），但事实证明，这成为了它的可取之处。 由于独立审查小组决定如何分配资金，他们的决定具有合法性。 最终，这种合法性阻止了立法者将基金会的资助决策置于直接政治控制之下。

马里兰大学科学史学家梅琳达·鲍德温 (Melinda Baldwin) 表示：“在很多方面，这实际上是科学家向其他利益相关者进行的推销，将同行评审纳入了科学的基石。”

英国在 20 世纪 80 年代末和 90 年代初也经历过类似的时刻，当时许多有争议的科学问题——从艾滋病毒到自闭症的病因，再到冷聚变——引起了媒体的广泛关注。 突然间，公众对区分合法科学和庸医产生了兴趣，许多科学组织回应说，“我们可以分辨什么是正确的科学，因为正确的科学是经过同行评审的，”费夫说。

如今，同行评审已成为标准。 期刊编辑要求大学教授在承担众多其他专业职责的同时撰写评论，而这些要求通常很快就会到来。 Lourido 估计他每个月会收到大约 10 个审稿请求，而实际上，他只有一两个时间。 作为加州大学旧金山分校免疫遗传学家（他除了担任期刊编辑之外）的一部分，麦克每一两天都会收到审稿请求。

这种节奏的部分原因是越来越多的人向期刊提交研究成果。 但 1960 年至 2020 年间，期刊数量也激增，其中一些定期出版“特刊”，研究人员为其生成定制内容。 许多期刊还发表了更多的手稿，因为它们现在只在网上发布，这使得编辑不必将一期文章放在有限的纸张上。

研究也越来越跨学科，这意味着许多研究需要更多的知识和时间来审查。 人工智能让研究人员更容易撰写他们的研究成果，也让世界各地的人们更容易向英文期刊提交论文，从而加剧了超载。 还有一些造纸厂或服务机构向绝望的研究人员收取费用，让他们将自己的名字印在伪造的（但通常看起来合法的）出版物上。

所有这些使得不仅难以维持同行评审的质量，而且难以确保同行评审的发生。 “有时我认为我们需要开始讨论出版业的低增长问题，”伊尔法努拉说。 “它已经像任何东西一样成长了。 这是极其不健康的！”

博客位于

人工智能研究人员敏锐地感受到内容爆炸式增长。 计算机科学家通常在会议论文集上发表论文，自 2019 年以来，提交给顶级人工智能会议的论文数量增加了 2 至 10 倍。 因此，经常会收到来自“对这个领域不够了解，无法进行评估或提供良好反馈”的人的评论，加州大学圣塔芭芭拉分校的计算机科学家 Haewon Jeong 表示。

人工智能研究人员有能力尝试不同的东西。 他们的领域是新的，发展速度快如闪电，而且大部分工作都是在学术界之外进行的，因此许多研究人员不需要正式的出版物来促进他们的职业发展。 在此背景下，博客蓬勃发展。 如今，“维护一个好的博客几乎就像拥有一个好的播客频道一样，”郑说。 “你的声音会被放大，你就会被人认识。”

许多博客都是由行业领袖撰写的，但一些学者也加入了这一潮流。 来自熨斗研究所 (Flatiron Institute) 的人工智能研究员 Helen Qu 非常讨厌提交会议论文这种无益的苦差事，因此她决定只在她的新博客上发布她的研究成果（她目前正在致力于利用博弈论来阻止人工智能的颠覆性行为）。

一个名为“AI Alignment Forum”的长期博客是由众多研究人员撰写的，其中包括许多学者，他们关心如何使人工智能安全并造福于人类。 人工智能联盟论坛没有进行同行评审，而是使用一种机制，允许成员对内容进行投票赞成或反对，并发表评论来解释他们的观点。

当然，并不能保证读者在投赞成票或反对票时投入了很多（如果有的话）思考。 “这是它的一大弱点，”运营人工智能联盟论坛的 Lightcone 基础设施公司首席执行官奥利弗·哈布里卡 (Oliver Habryka) 承认。

另一方面，帖子往往会比在期刊上收到的少数同行评审得到更多的反应。 读者可以在对评论作出反应后改变他们的投票。 人工智能联盟论坛试图强调高质量工作的另一种方式是重新审视今年的热门内容，并要求成员就其老化情况以及这些说法是否成立发表评论。

与传统出版相比，该系统具有多种优势。 首先，它的速度要快得多，这在快速发展的领域尤其重要。 通常，如果研究人员向传统期刊提交文章，“当你的文章通过同行评审时，它很可能已经过时了，”哈布里卡说。

但在 Habryka 看来，人工智能联盟论坛的一个更强大的优势也许是投票系统吸引了读者对好的研究和反对它的反对意见的关注。 如果没有这样的机制，许多研究人员将依靠社交媒体来强调即将发生的事情。 但这使得该领域的焦点集中在公司的一时兴起上，这些公司使用专有的、可能存在偏见且通常不透明的机制来决定哪些内容应该突出显示。 “我真的不希望我的领域的注意力集中在 Twitter 算法的下游，”哈布里卡说。

许多博客使用的口语写作风格也能引起注意，这有利有弊。 对于曲来说，这意味着当她在博客上发表文章时，她不必担心其他人会因为她的想法而受到赞扬，因为没有人会对她的作品抱有完全相同的个人倾向。 Jeong 认为，平易近人的风格可以使复杂的概念更容易理解。 “这很有价值，”她说。

但范德比尔特大学的哲学家大卫·托斯塔德警告说，可访问性可能会以牺牲严谨性为代价，口语写作可能会让有魅力的声音上升到顶峰，无论他们的工作质量如何。

托斯塔德说，远离同行评审也会孤立你的工作。 他研究长期主义：如何最好地保护未来的人民。 最近，许多长期主义者都在关注如何防止人工智能带来人类的灭亡，许多人在人工智能联盟论坛上发表了他们的研究成果。

这给托斯塔德带来了一个问题，他坚信同行评审，并且只在使用同行评审的场所发表文章。 引用未经同行评审的作品肯定会引起危险信号，因为他自己的作品必须经过这些场所的评审过程。 这意味着他无法引用其领域内的大部分工作。 “这是非常有限的，”他说。

哈布里卡说，五年前，这是一个比今天更严重的问题。 现在，大多数学科的审稿人都承认有多种方式可以发表合法的作品。 “我认为，你真正想在[机器学习]论文中引用的内容中，只有不到 50% 最终得到了适当的同行评审，”他说。

改变战术

由于同行评审仍然占用大量时间，许多研究人员正在寻找加快这一过程的捷径。 Frontiers 期刊的工作人员进行的一项调查发现，超过一半的同行评审员已经以某种方式将人工智能纳入该流程，可能至少部分是出于这个原因。

有一天，人工智能生成的评论可能会被视为例行公事且有益。 但目前，人工智能的使用方式经常被研究人员认为令人讨厌和不道德。 例如，莱顿大学的语言学家 Marijn van Putten 最初很高兴收到一篇评论，建议他在其出版物中引用一本特定的中世纪阿拉伯语手册，其中记载了古代宗教领袖对《古兰经》提出了特定的解释。 “我当时想，‘太好了，我要去查一下！’”他说。

但他无法在任何地方找到参考文献。 最后，经过两天的搜索，范·普滕开始考虑另一种可能性：人工智能产生了幻觉。 他回头查看评论，发现它确实包含人工智能生成文本的特征，例如无端使用破折号。 他通过人工智能检测工具运行该文本，该工具告诉他该文本几乎肯定是由人工智能生成的。 “这非常令人沮丧，而且浪费了我的时间，”他说。

新墨西哥理工学院的哲学家克里斯·乔格鲁克 (Chris ChoGlueck) 表示，除了产生幻觉的风险之外，将未发表的手稿上传到可能保留数据的聊天机器人还可能构成违反保密性。 本地运行的大型语言模型或同意不保留数据的服务可以提供解决方案，但它们要求那些愿意走捷径的人也表现出一定程度的谨慎。

今年，人工智能会议 NeurIPS 将进行一项试验，看看定制的人工智能工具是否可以帮助审稿人而不完全取代他们的判断。 例如，会议组织者在 NeurIPS 网站上写道，该工具可以帮助研究人员理解提交的内容并进行撰写评论所需的背景研究，但它本身不会撰写评论。

与此同时，许多领域正在尝试其他改革同行评审的方式。 解决审稿过程缓慢的一个长期策略是预印本，即研究人员在 arxiv.org 等网站上发布的正式书面出版物，以便他们的研究成果在通常的出版流程中可见。 预印本现在被视为某些领域资助和工作申请的合法依据，因为人们普遍认为，人们在等待正式出版时不应该暂停自己的职业生涯。

其他想法集中在审查过程本身。 一个明显的步骤是重新分配审核工作量以反映提交的来源。 编辑们往往不成比例地将审稿任务分配给来自美国和其他少数国家的男性研究人员，而不是公平地分配工作量。

一些研究人员还主张向同行评审员付费，尽管其他人担心这种做法会增加研究人员已经面临的繁重的出版费用。 有证据表明，每次审核 100 至 300 美元的报酬可以加快流程，同时又不会影响质量。 ChoGlueck 说，这可能是因为在等式中添加资金让人感觉“实际上有一个严格的截止日期”。

他建议，如果没有这种动机，一些审稿人可能会认为截止日期是“神奇的”，“因为你可以改变它们。”

其他人正在推动更多的结构性变革。 一种已经在有限范围内使用的选择是将同行评审过程与期刊提交分开。 相反，研究人员社区在正式提交论文之前对其进行审查，然后研究人员可以选择将论文提交给许多致力于发表以这种方式审查的研究的期刊。 如果第一个期刊决定不发表文章，作者可以联系第二个期刊，而无需接受新一轮的同行评审。

与此同时，学术传播倡导者卡梅伦·内伦(Cameron Neylon)长期以来一直公开质疑是否所有期刊文章都真的需要同行评审，因为最终对世界产生影响的论文很少。 他认为，也许研究在送去同行评审之前必须达到感兴趣的门槛。

面对所有这些压力和主张，同行评审是否已接近临界点，最终会失败吗？

很难想象全面放弃同行评审，因为该系统在大多数领域都根深蒂固，既是职业发展的一部分，也是获得公众信任的一种方式。 与此同时，如果学术出版继续以目前的速度增长，系统根本无法跟上。 “所以在某个时刻，有些东西会崩溃，”尼伦说。 他建议，也许研究领域应该找到方法来鼓励高质量的出版物而不是数量，而不是放弃同行评审。

考虑到目前的激励措施，很难想象研究人员会自愿减少发表论文。 但也许两者都会在某种程度上发生。 随着审稿人数量的减少，期刊将不得不遏制审稿人的激增，这可能会抑制出版物数量的增长。 与此同时，同行评审可能会变得不那么严格、更加碎片化，这种做法在不同领域具有不同的含义。

已经有证据表明后两件事正在发生。 过去，三名审稿人审稿是标准做法，但麦克说，他最近发现免疫学领域的平均审稿人数量接近两名。 在经济学领域，一些著名期刊已经向同行评审员支付费用。 与此同时，许多科学领域的研究人员经常发布预印本。

同行评审即使不是镇定自若，也是有弹性的。 这种做法可能会以一种或另一种形式继续存在，但它可能与我们习惯的同行评审不同。
